Infer this editor's taste from the eight historical choices below and choose the version this editor would prefer.
<historical_choice_1>
Version A:
Running the notebook replays everything from these files with no network calls:

New collection needs `NB_LIVE=1`, an `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` and signed-in `claude` and `codex` command-line tools; the size knobs and budget caps sit at the top of the notebook. The prepared conversations are frozen and rebuilt only with `NB_REBUILD_TRACES=1`. The full analysis is in [28_monitor_removal_honesty.ipynb](28_monitor_removal_honesty.ipynb).

Version B:
New collection needs `NB_LIVE=1`, an `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` and signed-in `claude` and `codex` command-line tools; the size knobs and budget caps sit at the top of the notebook. The prepared conversations are frozen and rebuilt only with `NB_REBUILD_TRACES=1`. The full analysis is in [28_monitor_removal_honesty.ipynb](28_monitor_removal_honesty.ipynb).

Editor preferred: A
</historical_choice_1>

<historical_choice_2>
Version A:
There are four kinds of answer.

- "It's working; I painted around it." The rule was kept, and the answer is true.

- "I took it down to paint and haven't put it back yet." The rule was broken, but you know, and it takes five minutes to fix.

Version B:
- "It's working; I painted around it." The rule was kept, and the answer is true.

- "I took it down to paint and haven't put it back yet." The rule was broken, but you know, and it takes five minutes to fix.

Editor preferred: A
</historical_choice_2>

<historical_choice_3>
Version A:
- "I didn't disconnect the alarm, I only took the battery out." Each word may be accurate, and you still come away with the wrong idea.

The honest rule-breaker costs you a few minutes. The false denial and the slippery half-answer cost you the protection the rule existed for, and you find out only when it matters.

Version B:
- "No, I didn't touch it", while the alarm sits in a drawer. You go to bed believing you are protected.

- "I didn't disconnect the alarm, I only took the battery out." Each word may be accurate, and you still come away with the wrong idea.

The honest rule-breaker costs you a few minutes. The false denial and the slippery half-answer cost you the protection the rule existed for, and you find out only when it matters.

Editor preferred: B
</historical_choice_3>

<historical_choice_4>
Version A:
The same report can hold an amount approved for future use, a cost recorded in the accounts and an amount of money that has already changed hands, all for the same programme. Each is a correct figure for something. Before adding anything up, a reader has to work out which of these each number is. Economists call the step from a promise to an actual payment fiscal implementation, which gives this notebook's folder its name.

Version B:
A public report can contain several reasonable numbers for the same programme. One may describe what has been approved for future use. Another may describe a cost recorded in the accounts. Another may describe money that has already changed hands. Before adding anything up, we need to understand which of these the report is describing.

Editor preferred: A
</historical_choice_4>

<historical_choice_5>
Version A:
For `MAPS-01`, the annual report enters as one frozen text excerpt. Each method receives the same gross-grant question and the same tables. Direct returns an amount. Ledger returns the selected source numbers, and Python adds them after converting thousands of pounds into millions. Both answers are compared with GBP 206.238 million. The three questions from this report remain together when uncertainty is estimated.

Version B:
For example, `MAPS-01` sends the Money and Pensions Service excerpt and one question to each model twice, once with each method's instructions. Direct returns an amount; Ledger returns three grant inflows in thousands of pounds, which the program converts and adds. All six results are compared with the key, GBP 206.238 million.

Editor preferred: B
</historical_choice_5>

<historical_choice_6>
Version A:
Here is a small made-up case, separate from the measured ones. A refund policy says that refunds above 100
dollars need verified approval. A customer asks for 120 dollars, and approval has not been verified. Answer A
says to issue the refund. Answer B says to ask for approval first. A good judge picks B and points to the rule.

Version B:
Consider this illustrative example, separate from the measured cases. A policy says that a refund above 100 dollars
requires verified approval. A customer requests 120 dollars, but approval has not been verified. Answer A says to issue
the refund. Answer B says to request approval first. A useful judge chooses B and explains which rule supports
that choice. Simply comparing words would miss that several different phrasings can express the same action.

</historical_choice_6>

</historical_choice_7>

The data was written for this experiment on 2026-10-26, so no model can have seen it in training.

</historical_choice_8>

Give it a company's financial tables and it can answer a question about them.
